q: Tell me about yourself and why you are interested in this ML/backend role.
followups: What did you enjoy least in your last project?
Where do you want to be in two years?
answer: Structure: present, past, future in about 90 seconds. Situation/present: 'I am a developer who has spent the last year building and deploying Python and FastAPI services and small ML pipelines.' Past: one or two concrete achievements with a measurable result ('I built a candidate-scoring API with tests and CI that cut manual triage time by about a third in a pilot'). Action link: what I learned (testing, reproducibility, monitoring). Future: why this role, tied to the company's work ('I want to own models in production end to end, and your team ships and monitors ML services'). Result: a clear ask or fit statement. Keep it specific, avoid reciting a CV, and end by inviting a question. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)

q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate about a technical approach.
followups: What if the data had shown they were right?
What if they still disagreed after the data?
answer: Situation: two of us disagreed on whether to add a cache layer or fix slow queries for a slow endpoint before a release. Task: reach a decision quickly without damaging the relationship, since I owned the endpoint. Action: I proposed we settle it with data instead of opinion: I profiled the endpoint, showing 80% of time in one unindexed query, and wrote down the criteria (latency target, risk, effort). We agreed to try the index first (one hour, reversible) and to revisit caching if the target was missed. I made sure their concern about future load was recorded as a follow-up. Result: p95 dropped from 1.4 s to 180 ms, the cache was not needed yet, and my teammate later reviewed the load-test plan. Reflection: separate the person from the idea, agree on evidence up front, and prefer reversible steps. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)

q: Describe a time you helped a less experienced colleague grow.
followups: How do you mentor someone who is defensive about feedback?
How do you balance mentoring with your own deadlines?
answer: Situation: a new junior developer on my team was submitting pull requests that repeatedly failed CI and needed heavy rework. Task: get them productive without taking over their work. Action: I paired with them for two short sessions on how to run the test suite and linters locally, walked through one of my own failed PRs to normalise mistakes, and set up a small checklist and pre-commit hooks. I gave review comments that explained the why and pointed to the docs rather than just fixing the code, and gave them one small independent ticket to own. Result: within a month their first-pass CI success rate rose from about 30% to 80%, review cycles dropped, and they later fixed a flaky test on their own. Reflection: teach the process, not just the answer, and make the safe path the easy one. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)

q: Tell me about a production incident you were involved in. What was your role and what changed afterwards?
followups: What would you do differently?
How did you decide rollback rather than fix forward?
answer: Situation: after a routine deploy of a model-serving API, error rates rose to 8% and latency doubled; I was on call. Task: restore service first, then understand the cause. Action: I declared an incident in the team channel, assigned a communicator so I could focus, and rolled back to the previous version within ten minutes, confirming recovery on the dashboard. Then I investigated with logs: a dependency upgrade had changed a default that made the model load on every request. I wrote a blameless postmortem with a timeline and five whys, and added a load test with a latency gate in CI, a readiness probe that checks the model is loaded, and a canary stage. Result: the customer impact lasted 25 minutes, similar regressions have since been caught in the canary, and mean time to rollback is one command. Reflection: mitigate before diagnosing, communicate early, and fix the process, not the person. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: Describing the fix but not the prevention

q: Tell me about a time you were given a vague task with unclear requirements. How did you proceed?
followups: What if the stakeholder cannot define success?
How do you handle changing requirements midway?
answer: Situation: I was asked to 'improve the search on the internal tool' with no metric or user list. Task: turn it into something deliverable within a sprint. Action: I talked to five users and read the search logs to see what failed (30% of queries returned nothing, mostly due to typos and abbreviations). I wrote a one-page problem statement with a proposed success metric (zero-result rate under 10%), options with effort and risk, and got the product owner's agreement before building. I shipped the smallest change first (fuzzy matching and synonyms) and measured it, keeping a list of what I deferred. Result: the zero-result rate fell to 9%, and the team adopted the one-pager format for vague requests. Reflection: clarify the outcome and the user, measure the current state, agree on a metric, then iterate in small steps. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)

q: Tell me about a significant mistake you made and what you learned.
followups: What would have happened if there was no backup?
How do you avoid over-correcting after a mistake?
answer: Situation: I ran a data migration script against a shared staging database instead of my local copy because I had a stale environment variable, overwriting test data other people depended on. Task: recover quickly and prevent it recurring. Action: I told the team immediately rather than hoping nobody noticed, restored from the nightly backup within 40 minutes, and apologised to the affected colleagues. I then made the script require an explicit `--env` flag and print the target host with a confirmation prompt for non-local databases, added a dry-run mode, and documented it. Result: no data lost beyond half a day of test changes, and the same safeguard was later reused in two other scripts. Reflection: own it early, fix the system that allowed the mistake, and build guardrails around destructive operations. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: A fake failure ('I work too hard')

q: Tell me about a time you had to push back on a stakeholder's request or deadline.
followups: What if they insisted on the original date?
How do you estimate under uncertainty?
answer: Situation: the product lead wanted a churn-prediction model in production in two weeks for a customer event. Task: protect quality and trust while still delivering value. Action: I explained what was feasible using a short plan: label definition and a leakage-safe split, baseline, then evaluation. I offered options with trade-offs: (A) a rule-based recency score in one week, (B) a first model with a limited pilot to 5% of users in four weeks, (C) the full model in eight weeks. I showed that shipping an unvalidated model risked wrong customers being targeted and lost credibility. Result: they chose A followed by B; the rule-based score already captured much of the value for the event, and the pilot showed a measured lift before we scaled it. Reflection: bring options and evidence, not just a no, and keep the stakeholder's goal in view. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: Agreeing and then missing the deadline silently

q: Describe a time you drove a change (a practice, a tool, a standard) across a team where you were not the manager.
followups: How did you handle the resisters?
How did you know it was worth the effort?
answer: Situation: our team deployed models manually and two incidents came from copying the wrong artifact. Task: introduce a safer release process without formal authority. Action: I measured the problem first (number of manual steps, time per release, past incidents), then built a small pilot: a script that pulled a registered model version, ran checks and deployed, tried on my own service for two releases. I demoed it, asked colleagues for concerns (they worried about losing flexibility, so I added an override with logging), and wrote a short guide. I asked one respected teammate to adopt it next, which built trust. Result: within six weeks four of five services used it, release time dropped from about 40 to 10 minutes, and there were no wrong-artifact incidents in the following quarter. Reflection: solve a shared pain, prove it small, listen to objections, and make adoption easy. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: Claiming credit for the whole team's work

q: You have three urgent asks in one week: a production bug, an analysis for the executive team, and a teammate's blocked review. How do you decide what to do first?
followups: What if all three are equally critical?
How do you say no to the fourth request?
answer: Situation: I faced exactly this: a bug affecting a subset of customers, a leadership request due Friday, and a colleague waiting on my review. Task: sequence work by impact and cost of delay, and keep people informed. Action: I assessed each quickly. The bug affected customers now, so it came first: I timeboxed diagnosis to two hours and posted status. The review took 20 minutes and unblocked someone else, so I did it between bug investigations because delay on a blocked colleague multiplies. For the analysis I confirmed the real deadline and scope with the requester, agreed on a simpler first version, and scheduled focused time. I told each person what to expect and when. Result: bug fixed the same day, review done on time, analysis delivered on Friday with agreed scope. Reflection: prioritise by user impact and cost of delay, favour small unblockers, and communicate trade-offs rather than silently dropping work. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: Working on everything and finishing nothing
Not telling anyone about the trade-off

q: Tell me about a time you noticed a problem that was not your responsibility but would hurt the business. What did you do, and how did you decide how far to go?
followups: What if the other team had ignored you?
When would you escalate to management?
answer: Situation: while monitoring my service I noticed another team's upstream feature pipeline had silently started sending null values for a key field; my model's predictions were degrading, and nobody had raised it. Task: get it fixed without overstepping and without letting customers keep getting worse results. Action: I checked the evidence (null rate jumped from 0.2% to 35% after a schema change), then contacted the owning team directly with a short, factual message including graphs and the time of change, and offered help. In parallel I added a temporary safeguard in my own service (fall back to the previous value and alert) to limit the impact. I followed up in their incident channel until they confirmed the fix and proposed a shared data contract with schema and null-rate checks at the boundary. Result: the upstream fix landed the same day, my safeguard was removed, and the contract check caught a similar issue two months later. Reflection: escalate with evidence, protect your own users, propose a durable fix, and stay within your remit by helping rather than changing their code. (Model answer: adapt to your own real story and numbers; do not memorise.)
pitfalls: Fixing their code without telling them
